pages.title: Into the Wilderness
pages.text: Mark says that after His baptism in the Jordan, the Spirit sent Him out into the wilderness. He was there forty days, with the wild animals, and angels served Him.
sources: Mark 1:9–13 (parallels Matthew 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13)
https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/moretto-da-brescia-christ-blessing-saint-john-the-baptist (the London companion: Christ just baptised, about to go into the wilderness)
Photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Jordan_River_at_Qasr_al-Yahud,_2019_(04).jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0)

image.caption: The Jordan at Qasr al-Yahud, where tradition places His baptism
image.credit: Photo: Bahnfrend, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pages.title: The Judean Desert
pages.text: The traditional wilderness is the dry country between Jerusalem and Jericho. It drops east to the Dead Sea, about 1,400 feet below sea level.
sources: https://www.britannica.com/place/Jericho-West-Bank (Dead Sea about 1,410 ft / 430 m below sea level; the hills of Judaea to its west)
UNESCO Tentative List, El-Bariyah: wilderness with monasteries (2012) — read via search index only
Photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Palestine,_Wadi_Qelt,_(Landscape_22).jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0)

image.caption: Wadi Qelt, a gorge running down toward Jericho
image.credit: Photo: Britchi Mirela, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pages.title: The Mount of Temptation
pages.text: Above Jericho is a mountain named for the forty days, Quarantania. Since the twelfth century, tradition has placed two of the temptations there. A Greek Orthodox monastery is built into its cliff.
sources: https://www.seetheholyland.net/mount-of-temptation/ (about 5 km north-west of Jericho; 'Mount Quarantania'; tradition from the 12th century; monastery rebuilt late 19th century)
Photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Monastery_of_the_Temptation_(Jeriho).jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0)

image.caption: The Monastery of the Temptation, built into the cliff
image.credit: Photo: Dmitrij Rodionov, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pages.title: The Painter
pages.text: Moretto da Brescia was born Alessandro Bonvicino around 1498. The nickname came from his grandfather. He lived and worked in Brescia, between Milan and Venice, and there is no record that he went to the Holy Land.
sources: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/437157 (Brescia ca. 1498–1554 Brescia)

https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/bonvicino-alessandro-detto-il-moretto-da-brescia_(Dizionario-Biografico)/ ('anni circa cinquanta' in 1548; 'figlio di Moretto, donde il soprannome'; documented trips only to Milan, Bergamo, Solarolo)
Photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Brescia_e_Monte_Guglielmo_dal_Castello.jpg (CC BY-SA 3.0)

image.caption: Brescia today, below the foothills of the Alps
image.credit: Photo by Wolfgang Moroder, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

pages.title: A City Sacked
pages.text: In 1512, when Moretto was about fourteen, French troops under Gaston de Foix sacked Brescia, then one of the richest cities in Lombardy. Britannica says it never recovered. He painted this picture a few years later.
sources: https://www.britannica.com/place/Brescia-Italy ('one of the wealthiest cities in Lombardy'; 'never recovered from its sack by the French under Gaston II, comte de Foix, in 1512')
https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/437157 (dated ca. 1515–20)
Photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Brescia_illustration_XVII.png (Public domain (PD-old))

image.caption: Brescia in an old engraving
image.credit: From Margaret L. Huggins, Gio. Paolo Maggini: His Life and Works (1894). Public domain.

pages.title: Brescia to Jerusalem
pages.text: Brescia is about 1,600 miles from Jerusalem. The tree in Moretto’s wilderness is a beech, which grows in European woods, not in the Judean desert. The Met reads it as a sign of Christ and of fasting, because hermits were said to live on its nuts.
sources: Great-circle distance Brescia (45.54, 10.22) – Jerusalem (31.78, 35.23): 2,638 km / 1,639 mi (Wikipedia coordinates)
https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/botanical-imagery-in-european-painting (beech: 'an attribute of Christ, and a symbol of abstinence'; nuts fed hermits)
Photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Lear_-_Lago_d%27Iseo_-_B1997.7.342_-_Yale_Center_for_British_Art.jpg (CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication))

image.caption: Lake Iseo, near Brescia, sketched by Edward Lear in 1867
image.credit: Edward Lear, Lago d'Iseo, 1867. Yale Center for British Art (B1997.7.342). CC0.

pages.title: Its Real Size
pages.text: The canvas is 18 inches high and 21¾ inches wide. The frame of light shows that size.
sources: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/437157 (oil on canvas, 18 x 21 3/4 in.)

pages.title: Hidden Angels
pages.text: The angels and cherubs were painted over at some point, to hide that the canvas had been cut down. A restoration in 1988 uncovered them. The cherubs probably surrounded a figure of God the Father, sending the angels to serve Christ.
sources: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/437157 (Catalogue Entry: angels and cherubim painted out, uncovered in the 1988 restoration; 'a radiance surrounding a figure of God the Father')

pages.title: A Fragment
pages.text: This was once part of a larger canvas. The faint cherubs at the left edge were cut through when it was trimmed, and the lost part probably showed other moments from Christ's life. A painting in London of Christ blessing John the Baptist may have come from the same canvas.
sources: https://metmuseum.org/toah/works-of-art/11.53 (a fragment of a larger canvas that continued past the cherubim at the left and showed other events from Christ's life)
https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/moretto-da-brescia-christ-blessing-saint-john-the-baptist (suggested to have been part of the same composition; figure sizes differ)
Photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Moretto,_cristo_che_benedice_il_battista.JPG (Public domain (PD-Art, PD-old-auto-expired))

image.caption: Moretto, Christ Blessing Saint John the Baptist, National Gallery, London
image.credit: Moretto da Brescia, Christ blessing Saint John the Baptist, National Gallery, London (NG3096). Public domain.

pages.title: A Rare Subject
pages.text: Few painters chose the forty days in the wilderness. Mark gives the scene two verses and says He was with the wild animals. Moretto filled the hills with them.
sources: https://www.metmuseum.org/en/essays/painting-the-life-of-christ-in-medieval-and-renaissance-italy (the unusual theme let Moretto fill the landscape with birds and animals)

pages.title: Made for Private Prayer
pages.text: The scholar Guazzoni groups it with three related pictures that were probably made for private prayer at home rather than for a church.
sources: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/437157 (References: Guazzoni 1981 groups it with works 'meant for private, domestic devotions')

pages.title: Where It Hangs
pages.text: The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York bought the painting in 1911. It is on view on Fifth Avenue.
sources: https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/437157 (Rogers Fund, 1911; on view in Gallery 611 as of 2026-11-11)
Photo: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art_-_Main_Building.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0)

image.caption: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Fifth Avenue, New York
image.credit: Photo: Yair Haklai, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
